title: Cleo's Chaotic Fete
markdown:
Gadzooks! Cleo the raven had an office door that read Cleo Nightingale, School Archivist, and a plan thick enough to stun a brick. Founder’s Day Fete was days away. No more near-disasters from Principal Higgins. No more glitter eruptions from Mrs. Gable. This year the whole carnival would run like clockwork, or Cleo would know why.

Her office perched above The Flourishing Loaf. Usually the cinnamon soothed her. Today it only made her talons drum faster.

“Theo,” she cawed, tight as a drawn string. “Section 3, subsection B. Celebratory balloons. Seventy-two percent helium, twenty-eight percent atmospheric air. Optimal buoyancy. Minimal drift. Seven committees. One schedule. No excuses.”

Theo, a seal whose fur was polished obsidian, blinked from the rug. “That sounds very precise, Cleo. Room for the unexpected?”

“Unexpected means disaster.” She tapped the leather-bound manual, pages packed with her neat black script. “Foolproof. Every volunteer. Every second. A flawless fete, or I shall eat my bow tie.”

The boast travelled. By dawn of the fete it had become a dare the school intended to test.

Cleo, sharp in a tiny bow tie, perched on the highest window. Volunteers clutched her manual like scripture. The band launched into the alma mater, spirited and wildly off-key.

Task one arrived wearing thorns. The decorations committee took “adorn all entranceways with natural flora” as a hunting licence and draped entire rose bushes over every doorway. Students ducked. A prefect yelped. Mrs. Gable, scenting chaos, advanced with a tub of emergency glitter.

Cleo’s first trick was to look as if she had ordered the ambush. “Living Thresholds,” she announced, dropping onto a bush as if it were a podium. “Page four. If you can get through without a scratch, you may have a jam tart. Higgins, the glitter stays in the tub or I file you under Confetti, Unauthorised.”

Mrs. Gable froze. Principal Higgins, who had been about to forbid the whole display, found himself holding a bush upright instead. The decorations team, robbed of their rivalry, began weaving the thorns into an arch because Cleo was already calling it one.

Task two wobbled into view: a towering monument of jam tarts, built by a zealous Year 7 who had read “abundant refreshments” and taken it personally. The stack leaned like a guilty secret. One tart escaped and fled toward the band.

“Communal Vertical Picnic,” Cleo said, as if the phrase had always lived in subsection C. “We do not fight a mountain. We eat our way to stability. Refreshments, you will supply plates. Decorations, you will supply the hungry. Theo—”

Theo, who understood balance the way other people understood chairs, organised the first careful collapse into a picnic. Sticky fingers replaced panic. The tart that had joined the band was declared a mascot and left on a snare drum, where it behaved better than the cymbals.

Task three had chemistry. The balloon brigade, faithful to the seventy-two percent instruction and faithless to the meaning of helium, had borrowed fizzy baking soda and vinegar from the Fun Science Corner. The balloons filled with rapidly expanding gas, bobbed, weaved, and bumped one another with soft squeaks. One particularly heroic balloon nudged Principal Higgins’s toupee clean off his head and sent it sailing toward the flagpole.

A cold wave hit Cleo. For a blink she was only an archivist watching her clockwork become a carnival.

Then she stole the disaster and named it.

“Rogue Balloon Roundup,” she cawed, as if subsection D had been waiting all term. “First to return the Principal’s weather gets extra tart. Second prize is not being chased by a squirrel.”

The squirrel on the flagpole had already entered. Higgins and the squirrel became unwilling partners in a hunt. The balloon brigade, who had expected disgrace, found themselves referees. Theo herded the squeakiest balloons into a corner that sounded, as he observed, like a band that had not yet learned the alma mater.

Cleo’s rivals turned on the problem instead of on her. Mrs. Gable used the glitter, at last, to mark the balloon course. Higgins, toupee restored by a confused squirrel and a polite thank-you, stopped quoting regulations and started counting scores.

Between the roundup and the tart crumbs, Cleo paused. The bakery’s cinnamon climbed the stairwell. Gold light lay on the playground like a cloth someone had remembered to spread. She watched Theo set a balloon gently on a bench, and for a few breaths she was not a conductor. She was a raven on a warm sill, letting the fete be noisy without her.

“I think,” she told Theo, when she found her voice again, “the manual was a little too detailed. And I didn’t account for how much fun it is to figure things out as you go.”

Theo’s smile was small and kind. “It has character. We could have used the tarts to prop the roses. Those balloons were trying to start a band.”

Volunteers adapted because she had given them permission dressed as a plan. Students rearranged the remaining thorns into an arch that almost looked intentional. Jam became a communal picnic. Cleo untangled strings, suggested a sturdier tart table, and even chuckled when Higgins retrieved his toupee from the squirrel a second time, with more dignity than the first.

As the sun went down in gold and rose, friends sat with jam-covered hands and stories that would outlast any schedule. Cleo was still the archivist. She was also, for one loud afternoon, the trickster who had bluffed a fete into belonging to everyone.

She filed the manual that evening under Suggestions, and if you asked whether she had meant the thorns, the tart mountain, and the airborne toupee, she would only settle her bow tie and wink.
